title: Parasympathetic Regulation
subtitle: Recovery, flexibility and state change
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating parasympathetic regulation across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain parasympathetic regulation in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in parasympathetic regulation.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to parasympathetic regulation.

sections.explainSimply: Parasympathetic processes support recovery after activation and help regulate heart rate, digestion and social engagement.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Regulation is not simply “turning on the vagus nerve”; it involves flexible coordination across autonomic, respiratory, cortical and contextual systems.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia and heart-rate variability index aspects of cardiac vagal control but are affected by respiration, posture, medication and fitness.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of parasympathetic regulation as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need parasympathetic regulation to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: HRV is not a direct measure of psychological safety.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use parasympathetic regulation to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses parasympathetic regulation to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: HRV is not a direct measure of psychological safety. Evidence classification: established physiology; measurement caveats.
